title: Kinetic particle theory & states of matter

items.stem: State three assumptions of the kinetic particle theory.
items.back:
1. All matter is made of tiny particles
2. Particles are always moving
3. Particles collide elastically (no kinetic energy lost overall)
items.frontier: Brownian motion — the random jiggling of pollen grains in water — was the first visible proof that liquid is made of moving particles (1827).

items.stem: State the arrangement and movement of particles in a solid.
items.back: close together in a regular arrangement; vibrate about fixed positions

items.stem: A gas is heated in a sealed container. Explain, using particle theory, why the pressure increases.
mark_scheme: particles gain kinetic energy / move faster
particles collide more frequently with walls
greater force per collision / harder collisions
items.frontier: Inside a car engine, gas pressure from combustion can exceed 100 atm — same principle.

items.stem: A drop of food colouring spreads faster in hot water than cold water. Explain this observation using the kinetic particle theory.
mark_scheme: in hot water, particles have more kinetic energy
particles move faster / collide more frequently

items.stem: The graph shows temperature vs time as a substance is heated continuously. Describe what is happening at region B.
mark_scheme: energy is used to break intermolecular forces/bonds, not raise temperature

items.stem: A student inflates a balloon and then places it in a bowl of ice. The balloon shrinks. Use kinetic particle theory to explain this observation. [6]
mark_scheme: ice cools the gas inside the balloon
fewer collisions per second with the inside of the balloon
external air pressure causes balloon to shrink
items.frontier: This is how liquid nitrogen (−196°C) can instantly shrink a balloon to a tiny fraction of its size.

items.stem: Discover how particle movement explains the behaviour of solids, liquids and gases.
items.learn_content:
Everything is made of particles. The state of matter depends on how much energy those particles have:

**Solid** → low energy, vibrate in place, regular arrangement
**Liquid** → more energy, flow past each other, irregular
**Gas** → high energy, move randomly at speed, far apart

Heat a substance → particles gain energy → eventually change state.
learn_steps: In which state are particles closest together? Why?
If you add heat to a liquid, what happens to the particles?
Why does ice melt at exactly 0°C — why not a range?
Name the three states in order of increasing particle energy.
